acceptance.summary: I read the full contract chain (02-audit.md rulings, 03-design-brief.md, platform constraints doc, STATUS.md ledger, round-1.md), read the generated README top to bottom as a native-English senior reader, inspected all 46 visual evidence files including every asset in both themes, the hero timeline frames, and the 890px/390px page captures in both themes, and read every load-bearing source file (snapshot.ts, material-change.mjs, readme.ts, checks.ts, validate-all.ts, both workflows, config.ts, profile.ts). All five gates pass on my machine: typecheck clean, 62/62 tests, validate (18 assets, 336.6 KB, 0 errors), render --check byte-stable, and qa:github against GitHub's real markdown API. Cross-consistency holds everywhere I probed: every README number traces to data/telemetry.json, alt text matches image content, the live GitHub account (verified read-only via gh) matches the snapshot exactly — 55 repos, all four featured descriptions, and even the "nine motion modules over a shared base" claim is literally true (10 files in src/motions, one is base.js). The hero entrance cascades correctly (identity before instruments, readouts staggered 900/960/1020ms, confirmed in both the shipped CSS and the t=1s frame), the light theme is genuinely ink-on-paper with the series ramp reversed, and round 1's claimed fixes are all verifiably in place. The automation is safe: paginated snapshot with loud sanity floors, distinct exit codes in the material-change guard, SHA-pinned least-privilege workflows that fully re-verify before committing. What remains is six minor polish items — a stale "Mission Control" source comment, a dead status config field, an unrecorded 58-to-55 account change between the audit and the snapshot, one stale line in the public cross-repo report, imported Title-Case copy in Active work, and a latent archived-repo divergence in a method line — none of which would stop a staff engineer from reading this as engineered-as-a-product. PASS.

findings.title: Banned-genre term "Mission Control" survives in a public source comment
findings.detail: The docblock reads "which repositories are promoted into Mission Control" — the exact vocabulary the audit ruled out (02-audit.md section 6.3 renamed the section to SELECTED SYSTEMS; MISSION CONTROL is build-failing lexicon per brief section 5.2). The validator lints the README and asset text manifests but not source comments, so it cannot catch this. The provenance footer explicitly invites readers into the source, so a careful reviewer will see the one phrase the whole project was built to purge. Verify: grep -rni 'mission.control' src/.
findings.recommendation: Reword the comment to "promoted into Selected systems".

findings.title: Dead `status` field in FeaturedRepoConfig is never consumed
findings.location: C:\GitHub\hakanduyar\src\shared\config.ts lines 31-36 and the four `status:` entries
findings.detail: `status: 'ACTIVE' | 'STABLE' | 'ARCHIVED'` is declared and populated on all four featured repos but consumed by nothing (grep confirms no reader in src/, scripts/, or tests/). It is dead configuration surface in a project whose round-1 resolution claims dead modules were deleted, and it is precisely the "operational status" register the audit banned from display — currently harmless only because nothing renders it.
findings.recommendation: Delete the field and its four values, or wire it to a real consumer if one is planned.

findings.title: 58-to-55 repository delta between the audit and the shipped numbers is not recorded anywhere
findings.detail: The audit's canonical table says 58 repos / 962 commits / TypeScript 62.9% / 136 contributions; the shipped page says 55 / 870 / 64.2% / 135. The live account (verified via GraphQL) is 55: AkademiGrup96, crm-fe and medyanes360-smartboardapplication were deleted or made private after the audit's evidence capture, on the same calendar day. The snapshot is right to trust the live measurement (RULE 3), but no ledger entry or note records that the account changed under the project, so both binding documents now disagree with the product on every headline number with no written explanation — the one gap in an otherwise immaculate provenance trail.
findings.recommendation: Add one line to the STATUS.md deviations ledger noting the owner removed three repositories after the audit evidence was captured, with the repo names and the resulting number shifts.

findings.title: Public audit-trail report carries a pre-fix repository description
findings.detail: The report's After column reads "Composable GSAP motion system for a production storefront - ten motion modules behind one declarative config", but round 1 corrected the live description to "...for a storefront - nine motion modules over a shared base..." (verified live via gh; telemetry.json and README match the corrected form). Since the .ai/ trail ships publicly as part of the provenance argument (ledger item 12), the shipped record contradicts itself on both the "production" overclaim and the module count that round 1 explicitly fixed.
findings.recommendation: Append a one-line note to cross-repo.md recording that the description was revised during review round 1, or update the table with a dated correction.

findings.title: Imported repo-description copy breaks the page's register in Active work
findings.location: C:\GitHub\hakanduyar\README.md, Active work section, spark bullet
findings.detail: "**spark** — Personal Planning, Focus, and Growth System. Last push 2026-07." is the GitHub description verbatim: Title Case marketing phrasing on a page that is otherwise rigorously sentence-cased and declarative. Relatedly, description-derived strings use spaced hyphens ("for a storefront - nine motion modules") where curated copy uses em dashes, so two dash conventions coexist within single sections. Generated verbatim by scripts/generate/readme.ts from telemetry.recentPushes[].description.
findings.recommendation: Either update the spark repository description to sentence case (additive, same owner) or have readme.ts prefer curated FEATURED_REPOS headlines when a recent-push repo is also a featured repo (both currently are).

findings.title: Latent divergence: commits method line counts all repos, commit sum excludes archived ones
findings.location: C:\GitHub\hakanduyar\scripts\generate\snapshot.ts (repos = nodes.filter(!isArchived)) vs scripts\generate\readme.ts telemetry table ("default branches, ${t.publicRepos} public repositories")
findings.detail: totalCommits and language bytes are summed over non-archived repos only, while publicRepos (used in the README method column and hero) is repositories.totalCount, which includes archived repos. Today the account has zero archived repos so both read 55 and every number is consistent; the day one repo is archived, the commit total silently excludes it while the method line still claims all 55 — an honesty drift the sanity floor would not catch. snapshot.ts itself uses repos.length for methods.totalCommits, so the snapshot and the README generator would also disagree with each other.
findings.recommendation: Emit the repo count used for the commit sum (repos.length) into telemetry and have readme.ts use that in the Commits method cell, or drop the isArchived filter since publicRepos already includes archived repositories.

findings.title: Material-change whitelist can leave the activity strip stale indefinitely
findings.detail: contributions and activity.weekly are excluded from the material view. The comment asserts "Owner-driven changes always also touch one of the whitelisted fields", but contributions that do not push to a default branch of an owned public repo (PRs/issues on other people's repositories, non-default-branch pushes) change the activity data without touching any whitelisted field, so the rendered strip and its caption would not refresh until some unrelated public push occurs. The no-metronome trade-off is deliberate and documented, but the stated invariant is slightly stronger than what the code guarantees.
findings.recommendation: Either soften the comment to state the known exception, or include activity.total in the material view (it only changes when real contributions occur, though it also shifts as the window slides — if that is the concern, document the exception instead).

completeness.summary: I read the audit rulings and full backlog, then checked every ticket against the repository at C:\GitHub\hakanduyar, ran the verification commands (render --check: 18/18 assets match source; validate: 0 errors, 336.6 KB; vitest: 62/62 pass; typecheck clean; README regeneration is a no-op; live qa:github pass against GitHub's Markdown API), and probed the live account with gh. The build system itself is complete, deterministic and self-checking, the round-1 resolution ledger's claims spot-check true in today's code (900/960/1020ms stagger present, PostgreSQL/nine-modules copy corrected at source, SHA-pinned workflows, material-change exit codes, pagination, font licences vendored), and descriptions plus topics are live on all four featured repositories. But the delivered product is incomplete on its own terms: all seven project commits sit on the local feat/hdu-profile-system branch which does not exist on origin, origin/main still serves the old Turkish README, T-012 (publish + live verification + sign-off) was never started, and neither workflow has ever run — so T-010's run-dependent acceptance criteria are unmet and the scheduled refresh is inert until a merge to the default branch. The project's own completion rule (a ticket is DONE only with an independent PASS on file) is satisfied nowhere: round-1 returned FAIL on all six dimensions and no round-2 review exists, leaving every Definition-of-Done category without independent PASS evidence. The GitHub profile bio, an explicit T-008 acceptance criterion and T-012 publish precondition, is verified null on the live API. Several promised artefacts are absent without a deviations-ledger entry (link check, docs/tokens.md, .gitattributes/.editorconfig, token-strategy record, committed CSP probes), and two evidence artefacts are stale relative to the final commits. Verdict FAIL because the publication half of the promise — and the project's own gate for calling anything done — is missing.
